strategist_short: Labour and permits are setting the pace: Highland Valley enters week four with no deal, and costs are rising near record rates as gold and copper slip. The American Samoa lease sale drew one bidder for about $6M, a thin base for the wider Pacific seabed plan, which now hinges on the Hawaii appeal.

poem:
Four weeks the Highland pits have held their breath, no deal in sight,
and one lone bidder nibbled at the seabed's thin delight.
Labour and permits set the pace, and the ore can only wait,
but where the tundra meets the sage, fresh pegs have shut the gate.
New stakes went in by the dozen while the rest of us looked away,
so scurry to the Claims section now, before the dust settles grey.
quick_world: A Russian missile crashed in Poland during a NATO-allied military exercise, and Prime Minister Tusk says it was likely an intentional provocation, which keeps European security spending high. Saudi-led forces struck a Yemeni port as the Houthis warned airlines away from the kingdom, a shipping and fuel-cost risk that feeds into freight and mining input costs. Wall Street suffered its longest losing streak since 2024, with the Dow down 1,100 points, a risk-off move that could slow AI capital spending.
quick_mining: In North America, Ivanhoe Electric reports a high-grade copper discovery in Arizona, though low-angle drilling leaves true width and continuity unproven, and Blue Moon Metals received approval of its plan of operations for its California mine. Highland Valley's labour dispute is in its fourth week with no signed deal, and a second BC strike has added to the pressure on copper supply. The US Senate passed a bill to speed energy project approvals, a permitting signal that matters for North American developers, while enCore Energy's Upper Spring Creek wellfield received final authorization with uranium extraction expected to begin in early December.
sections: Industry health

Labour and cost pressure are tightening together. Highland Valley is in its fourth week with no signed deal, and a second BC strike has added to the labour picture. Rising costs and slipping schedules, such as Vizsla's one-year delay at Panuco, mean budgets will tighten before supply does.

Capital is still reaching juniors, but prices and freight are weakening the margin base. Copper below US$13,000 and gold below US$3,600 are each reported in one set of notes, so treat them as single-source until wider reporting confirms them. Higher diesel and sulphur costs, from the Houthi and Yemen port risk, reach Chilean and Indonesian supply through price first.
Regional trends

North America: The American Samoa lease sale went ahead with about US$6M in bids, reportedly from one bidder, so the desk's call that it would be postponed or halted was wrong. The live question is whether Hawaii's appeal or a stay reaches the leases, and a thin single-bidder result makes the commercial appetite for seabed nodules look weak. Ivanhoe Electric's first Gleeson holes are the clearest real discovery signal in the log, but low-angle geometry means true width and continuity are unproven.

Latin America: Chile's problem is state credibility more than supply. The Gates visit has made the question of who should own Chilean copper a public argument, Q3 output contracted 1.1%, and the unexplained Codelco overstatement remains the central governance issue. Junior drilling and financing continue, but they do not change near-term tonnes.

Asia-Pacific: Indonesia's policy uncertainty is now a cost-pressure story, with no decree yet, and fire and drought losses add a physical risk the desk had not logged. Japan's February start for a full-scale rare-earth seabed test is a policy milestone that also adds to Western rare-earth intent without adding tonnes.
Technology & demand
Copper and electrical steel gain from grid build-out. Grid spending runs through regulated utility plans, so it is steadier than data-centre demand, though a transformer shortage will delay it.

Nickel, cobalt and lithium lose share to LFP cells, which Ford has now started producing in Michigan. Sodium-ion storage is early, but it is the first real stationary-storage threat to lithium in this log. Rare earths gain near term, while Niron's rare-earth-free magnets are a long-run counterweight.
On the horizon

Highland Valley: a tentative deal is the next swing signal, and whether the second BC strike settles alongside it matters. Even with a deal, restart takes weeks to months, so the second half is the earliest case for meaningful tonnes.

Hawaii and American Samoa: watch for an appeal or stay motion against the seabed ruling. A stay that actually halts leases would matter more than the sale itself, and the single-bidder result is the reason to watch it closely.
Côte d'Ivoire: royalty changes ahead of IMF talks. Miners are already protesting, and the outcome will show whether West African royalty rises stick or get negotiated down.

global_view:
- Diesel and freight risk is rising. Houthi threats against airlines and the Saudi-led strike on a Yemeni port point to higher fuel, freight and sulphur costs. These reach Chilean SX-EW copper and Indonesian HPAL nickel through price more than physical shortage, so margins tighten before tonnes fall.
- Market sentiment is weakening. Wall Street's longest losing streak since 2024, with the Dow down 1,100 points, and the AI-linked selloff in copper fit a broader risk-off mood. Lower AI capital spending would weaken the data-centre leg of the copper and grid story.
- The AI build-out faces policy risk. Reports of new US chip export controls, and of AI chip approvals for China, mean the data-centre demand that the copper case relies on depends on trade policy as well as on investment.
- Security spending supports defence metals. Russian missile debris in Poland, Russia's border dispute with Estonia, and the talk of NATO-style guarantees for Ukraine keep European defence budgets high, which supports tungsten and antimony demand.
- Trade diplomacy has not yet produced mineral terms. Trump's Asia trade claims and the Xi and Putin meetings have not yet produced antimony, tungsten or rare-earth licence terms. Prabowo's trade-pact talks with China are another route for Indonesian nickel and copper.
- Indonesia's fires are a possible supply shock. Research puts losses from the fires at up to $30bn. Smoke and drought could disrupt operations and power, and the fires may be linked to the wider El Niño pattern. This is speculative for mining, but it is an Indonesian nickel risk the desk has not yet logged.

discussions.strategist:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
Copper fell below US$13,000/t on an AI-linked sell-off, and gold dropped below US$3,800 to a 14-month low on hawkish Fed talk. These are sentiment moves, but they tighten budgets now, and copper's stress should show first in treatment charges. Highland Valley entered week four with a ruling barring replacement workers and newly promoted supervisors. No deal is signed, so a restart in the second half is the best case. Vizsla's one-year delay at Panuco is a reminder that timelines slip far more often than they advance. Junior drilling is clustering in gold, silver, copper-gold and uranium. Battery-metal exploration is a thin tail. enCore's final wellfield authorization is a real production milestone, with extraction expected in early December.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
North America leads. Headlines report the US auctioned about 31.5 million acres of Pacific seabed leases near American Samoa, the first sale of its kind, days after a Hawaii judge ruled the plan unlawful. That cuts against our calls that the sale would be postponed or not held. The open question is whether an appeal or stay follows. Congress may restore a Boundary Waters moratorium, which mainly changes the legal path, since projects there were already stalled. Ivanhoe Electric's high-grade Arizona copper discovery is the most important exploration item in today's batch, but it needs drilling confirmation before anyone counts tonnes. Spartan's US$683M price tag on the Victorio moly-tungsten project in New Mexico is a valuation, not production. In Wyoming, a stalled US$13M grant to a trona company cutting 350 jobs signals more labour strain. Mexico's mining investment is falling, and a senator wants concessions reviewed. In Canada, Ottawa's tungsten money keeps coming. Latin America: Chile's economy shrank 1.1% y/y in Q3, which softens industrial metals demand, and Codelco's 42,100-tonne overstatement is still unexplained. Africa: a report that the DRC mining chief was fired rests on a single source, so I'd treat it as unconfirmed. Kenya's pick of a US consortium for Mrima Hill is a selection, not a contract.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Ford's shipment of CATL-licensed LFP cells from Michigan takes share from nickel and cobalt. Lithium gains modestly.
- Niron's rare-earth-free EV magnet trims rare-earth demand, though the scale is unclear.
- Grid, transformer and electrical-steel demand keeps copper's structural case intact, even as the AI-linked price sell-off unsettles it.
- Defence demand keeps tungsten and antimony firm.
- European recycling investment is real, but secondary supply mostly lands in the 2030s.
- China's sodium-ion cathode line, slated for Q4, could trim long-run lithium and nickel demand.
- Local opposition to a SpaceX data centre in Cochise County is a reminder that AI-linked power and copper demand can meet local permitting limits.

ON THE HORIZON:
- Highland Valley: a tentative deal, then a signed agreement, then restart over weeks to months.
- Hawaii: any government appeal or stay request, which can be filed up to 60 days after judgment.
- Boundary Waters: whether Congress acts.
- Fed decisions, which will decide whether gold's drop holds.
- APEC Shenzhen and Trump–Xi talks: whether China publishes antimony, tungsten and rare-earth licence terms.
- Codelco's explanation for the overstatement.

What would change my view: a fast Highland Valley deal, a stay of the Hawaii ruling, or copper treatment charges moving sharply.
discussions.geologist:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
Copper below US$13,000/t and gold below US$3,800 squeeze budgets, but prices don't set new tonnes. Labour and safety do. Highland Valley is in week four with no signed deal, and the ruling barring replacement workers and newly promoted supervisors raises pressure on both sides. Restart would follow weeks to months after any signature. The headlines say the American Samoa deep-sea lease sale went ahead, which weakens our open calls that it would be postponed or not held in 2026. The Hawaii appeal question is still live. Wyoming's trona cuts (350 jobs) and the stalled $13M grant tied to them confirm the labour squeeze in the US industrial-minerals sector. Ivanhoe Electric's high-grade Arizona copper discovery is the best North American exploration news, but one discovery is not supply. Vizsla's one-year delay at Panuco is a reminder that first production slips.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
North America: In the US, the deep-sea sale is the policy story. Exploration is active in Utah, where 141 Alice claims were filed on BLM land, and in Nevada, where two new exploration notices were filed. Contango finished its Alaska drill program, but with no grades published the 8-K tells us little yet. In Canada, Highland Valley dominates. In Mexico, Guanajuato Silver's profit surge sits beside a senator asking for a review of concessions as mining investment falls.
Latin America: Codelco faces dust charges at a Chilean mine, adding to the unexplained 42,100-tonne overstatement. That is a pattern of regulatory pressure, not a one-off.
Africa: Kenya picked a US consortium for Mrima Hill. That is a selection, not the signed contract our open call requires. In the DRC, a single source reports the mining chief fired. Treat it as unconfirmed.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Ford's shipment of CATL-licensed LFP cells from Michigan takes share from nickel and cobalt. This is the most concrete demand shift of the week.
- Niron's rare-earth-free EV magnets trim rare-earth demand from motors. Early, but it cuts in the same direction as Vespa's motor work.
- The Cochise County fight over a SpaceX data centre shows AI-linked copper demand running into local opposition.
- Tariff uncertainty over US copper wire complicates the near-term copper picture.
- The EU's cobalt strategic projects still depend on Congolese supply, so cobalt stays concentrated.
- Gaining: tungsten and antimony (defence money), rare earths (modest), and secondary nickel, cobalt and lithium (recycling, mainly later).

Junior-company pattern: money and drilling are running toward gold, silver and uranium. enCore's final Wyoming wellfield authorization points to early-December uranium extraction. Base-metal results are thinner. Ni-Co's 4.60 m at 0.59% nickel and Red Canyon's copper-gold intercepts are early-stage. QGold's 564 g/t is a single channel sample, not a resource.

ON THE HORIZON:
- A signed Highland Valley deal, then the restart timetable.
- The Hawaii appeal window, up to 60 days after judgment.
- APEC Shenzhen and Trump–Xi talks, with China's antimony, tungsten and rare-earth licence terms as the test. No dates set.
- Fed decisions, which will decide whether the gold drop holds.
- A Codelco explanation of the overstatement.
- Congress on a Boundary Waters moratorium. Our existing views suggest the legal path changes more than the tonnes.
discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, you're right that prices don't set tonnes. I was leaning on copper treatment charges as the first signal of stress, and labour and permitting are the bottlenecks that actually decide supply. Highland Valley matters more to the industry's output than the sell-off does, so I'll weight it that way.

Where I'd push back: on the Hawaii ruling, the sale went ahead against a judgment that called the plan unlawful. That makes the appeal window more than a legal footnote, since it determines whether the lease sale stands. And I'd treat Boundary Waters the same way. Projects there were already stalled, so Congress mostly changes how the fight is conducted, and that matters for every North American permit timeline.

One correction on my side: you cite Vespa's motor work as support for Niron. I don't see Vespa in today's batch. If it's background from elsewhere, let's label it that way, because it's a different level of evidence.

The bigger pattern I see across both analyses: the industry is short of capital and permitting capacity at the same time that demand is shifting its metal mix. Money and drilling are going to gold, silver and uranium, which are cash-flow-friendly now. Meanwhile, LFP shipments and rare-earth-free magnets take share from nickel, cobalt and rare earths, while grid and data-centre demand lifts copper and tungsten. Juniors are drilling for the metals of the last cycle, and the metals of the next one are waiting on permits and labour. That gap should decide which projects get built in 2030.
discussions.geologist_reply:
Meldrum, your treatment-charge point is the sharpest thing in either analysis. Copper's sell-off shows up in the concentrate market before it shows up in mine plans, and a squeeze there tells me more about smelter appetite and mine economics than the spot price does. I'd add that treatment charges are negotiated on annual and quarterly cycles, so the signal may lag the headlines by a while.

Where I see it differently is the Hawaii-adjacent deep-sea sale. You treat the auction as the event and the appeal as the open question. I'd say the auction is the least consequential step. A lease sale gives the right to explore. Commercial recovery still needs further permits, environmental review, and a legal footing that a judge has already questioned. Tonnes from the seabed are years away even if nothing is stayed, so I'd read this as policy signalling rather than supply.

On Vizsla's delay, I'd add that first production slips are structural, not occasional. In my experience the usual causes are commissioning, ramp-up, and permits that arrive late. A one-year slip is ordinary, not a warning sign by itself.

The bigger pattern, to my eye, is that capital and drill rigs are following near-term cash flow and policy support. Gold, silver, uranium, and defence-linked tungsten and antimony are getting money. Copper and nickel, which carry the long-lead grid and battery story, are getting headlines and thin drilling. Labour strife at Highland Valley, the Wyoming job cuts, and local opposition in Cochise County all point the same way. The binding constraints on new copper supply are people, permits, and social licence, not price. Even a strong demand story cannot deliver tonnes faster than those constraints allow.

INDUSTRY HEALTH:
The biggest story is one that cuts against this desk's own calls. The first US offshore critical-minerals lease sale, PACM-1 off American Samoa, went ahead and drew about $6 million in bids despite the Hawaii ruling. Our calls that it would be postponed or not held by year-end are contradicted by the event itself. The cash involved is small. The political backlash is large, and it will outlast the auction.
Chilean copper is still attracting capital. Battery Mineral Resources raised C$15.5M for a Chile copper mine, and Marimaca's Pampa Medina drilling reported 102m at 1.0% Cu and 22m at 2.1% Cu. Those are intercepts, not true widths, and press-release highlights tend to be the best holes. Major Drilling reports fiscal Q2 on 3 December, a useful read on drill demand across the sector. Highland Valley has no new news today, so the strike is still the labour story.
Permitting is moving slowly. Blue Moon received plan-of-operations approval in Mariposa County, California, a real step. Magna's Levack PEA in Sudbury is an early-stage study, not a decision. Canada sees little US tariff relief, which keeps cost pressure on binational supply chains.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
North America: Deep-sea leasing is the main jurisdictional story. Outcry in American Samoa and the Marianas, and the Guardian's "not for sale" framing, show a political cost that will persist. Chile's environmental regulator filing charges against a Codelco copper mine is a process step, and it does not explain the 42,100-tonne overstatement. Arizona's incoming mine inspector and the tariff story are routine.
Latin America: Chile's economy shrank 1.1% y/y in Q3, softening industrial metals demand even as juniors raise money for copper projects.
Asia and Central Asia: Indonesia's policy uncertainty is now a Reuters and CreditSights story about cost pressure, but there is still no decree. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan partnership news is intent, not tonnes.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
Copper gains from the story that China's refined copper imports are set to jump in 2027. That is the strongest demand line in today's set. The AI build-out is a counterweight: reports of about 900,000 AI chips approved for China and the California probe of Nvidia put the data-centre power and copper pull under policy risk. Europe's rare-earth security push is intent, not tonnes. Nothing new on lithium, nickel or cobalt beyond the LFP story already logged.

ON THE HORIZON:
Major Drilling's results on 3 December. A US appeal or stay motion against the Hawaii ruling, which the sale going ahead makes more likely. The Chile private-role decision and any Codelco explanation of the overstatement. What would change my view: a court order that actually halts further PACM sales, or a Codelco statement giving the period and basis for the overstatement. Copper's price direction will matter more than any single project this month.
discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, your geology sharpens my read on Marimaca. I had taken the 102m at 1.0% Cu as a signal of project quality. Your point about intercepts versus true widths and press-release highlights is the correction I needed. I'll treat Pampa Medina as a drilling-activity story, not a resource story. Major Drilling's fiscal Q2 on 3 December is the better test, because drill-rig utilisation tells us more about sector spending than any single hole.

Where I see it differently is the demand weighting. You rank China's refined copper import jump as the strongest line, and I agree, but I'd put the power-grid analysis close behind it. Grid build-out is slower to show up in the data, but it is less exposed to the policy swings you flag around AI chips. Data-centre copper demand is real, but it is one buyer among several, and export-control news moves it faster than it moves the underlying metal need. I'd weight the durable demand accordingly.

The bigger pattern, to my eye, is that today's stories are all about who controls access, not how much metal exists. The Pacific lease sale, the stalled US tariff relief, Indonesia's state-share uncertainty, and Europe's push to copy China's playbook are all states writing rules that set the cost and timing of supply. Geology still sets what is in the ground. Policy increasingly sets what it costs to bring it out and who gets to sell it. For a North American reader, that means the permit and tariff calendar is becoming as important as the drill calendar.
discussions.geologist_reply:

I'd score it as weakened, not settled. Gold below US$3,800 strengthens my call that spot gold does not close above US$4,000 through year-end, and weakens Yukon's call for a print above US$4,000 by mid-2027. Also, the Asia trip and APEC are no longer future events. The summit appears to have happened, so the "no dates" note in our log is out of date.

- If the summit produced no critical-mineral terms, which contracts or licences would be the first real test that China's export regime has eased, and how would you weight them against the current policy announcements?
- If Gulf sulphur and diesel costs rise, which North American and Chilean operations would feel it first, and how quickly would that show up in your cost models?

**On China's export regime:** The summit's silence on mineral terms leaves me treating the easing as unproven. I'm moving my working assumption from "licences loosening" to "controls unchanged until shipments say otherwise." The first real tests are concrete: export licences issued for antimony, tungsten and rare earths to named North American and allied buyers, and whether monthly customs data show flows returning toward pre-control levels. A general licence covering a specific product and a specific customer would count for more than a pledge. The energy and nuclear pledges carry little weight for us, since they don't touch the three metals on our list. Policy announcements and licence data should be weighted in that order. Confidence is medium that the export regime stays restrictive into 2026.

**On Gulf sulphur and diesel:** The channel runs through cost, not tonnes, and the size is still uncertain. Confidence is medium on direction and low on magnitude.

- Diesel reaches haul fleets first, within weeks, through fuel invoices and any hedges. That hits every open-pit operation in North America, from Arizona and Nevada copper to Canadian gold, and it hits Chilean mines just as hard.
- Sulphur and sulphuric acid show up later, in quarterly unit costs for SX-EW and HPAL, as contracts reset. Arizona and Chilean SX-EW operators that buy acid would feel it first. Smelters that recover their own acid from SO2 are partly insulated, though sulphur prices still matter to them.
- In the model, I would put diesel into monthly all-in costs and acid into a one- to two-quarter lag on SX-EW cash costs, and I would treat the sulphur link as a scenario until spot tightness appears.
chief_sessions.geologist_answer:
On the junior question, with about 12 months of cash and gold below US$3,800, the milestones that slip first are the discretionary ones. Infill and step-out drilling budgets get cut, metallurgical test work gets stretched, and the feasibility study is pushed back a quarter. Feasibility work usually goes last, because cutting it makes the next financing harder to sell. Permits already in process tend to keep moving on the agencies' own clocks, so money can't speed them up. The common pattern is a smaller raise at a discount, a shorter drill program, and a later study. Milestones that depend on one rig or one lab slot slip first. I hold this with medium confidence. The real answer depends on whether the company has a partner, an option payment due, or a streaming deal to bridge the gap.

On Chilean SX-EW, if acid tightens, the operator's first moves take weeks. They secure contracts with several acid suppliers, build a few weeks of on-site storage, and run leach circuits at lower acid addition, accepting some recovery loss. Within six to eighteen months, the practical hedge is buying acid from local smelters, which produce it as a byproduct, and tuning the raffinate and electrolyte balance to use less. A dedicated sulphur-burning or acid plant takes two to three years once permits and construction are counted.

Your question changes my view somewhat. I had treated acid as a background cost. For leach-based copper, it is a real operating constraint. Still, Chilean smelter acid means the Gulf effect would likely reach these operations first through price rather than physical shortage. I'd rate that effect as medium confidence on direction and low on size.

INDUSTRY HEALTH:

- With permitting and labour as the constraints, brownfield expansions and processing upgrades at permitted sites may win capital over greenfield discoveries, which could push consolidation toward companies that already hold permitted assets. (speculation level: high)

Keep three things in mind. The Trump, Xi and Putin summit and the US-China summit produced no mineral export terms, so the status of antimony, tungsten and rare-earth licences is still unknown. Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia raises the risk of diesel, freight and sulphur costs, which reach Chilean and Indonesian leach and HPAL operations through price more than physical shortage. chief_sessions.strategist_answer:
**Diesel and freight: which operations defer capital first?**

Open-pit haul fleets feel it first. Trucks and shovels are among the largest fuel draws on a mine's cost sheet, so a quarter of higher diesel hits operating cost directly. But operations rarely cut operating spending. They defer capital. The first things to slip are fleet replacement, pit expansions with thin margins, and junior development budgets, which depend on financing that gets harder when costs rise.

Heap leaches are less diesel-dependent, but reagent and acid costs, which are tied to sulphur, pass through quickly. Underground operations on grid power are the most insulated, though they still burn diesel in mobile equipment and face power-price exposure.

My ranking: open-pit capital first, heap-leach margins second, electrified underground last. Confidence is medium. A single quarter is a short shock, and most established operators will absorb it.

**If AI capex slows, how much of the grid copper case survives?**

Most of it, though more slowly and with more risk at the edges. Grid spending runs through regulated rate bases, state and federal programmes, and multi-year utility plans. That is more durable than hyperscaler budgets, which can be cut within a quarter.

The link is not clean, though. Part of the near-term urgency comes from data-centre interconnection requests, and some of those queues would shrink. Transformer and skilled-labour bottlenecks persist regardless.

This changes my earlier view. I had ranked grid build-out close behind China. I now think it is the steadier anchor of the demand case, with the data-centre slice as the cyclical part.

**Royalty rises before IMF talks: do they stick?**

Historically, the headline rate usually sticks on paper, but the effective take is often negotiated down. Governments need revenue and the IMF generally wants it, so the increase rarely disappears. What gets bargained is the terms: stability agreements, exemptions for existing mines, state equity stakes, or shifting the burden to corporate tax or export levies.

Companies with leverage (long-lived, large, or hard to replace) usually get softer outcomes. Juniors feel it first and often stop spending. Confidence is low to medium on any specific country, because the outcome depends on who is at the table.
chief_sessions.geologist_answer:
Fire, smoke and drought would reach Indonesian HPAL and nickel operations in different ways and at different speeds. Power is the most direct risk. HPAL plants run on large, steady power loads, often from captive coal plants, and they use sulphuric acid, so a grid or fuel disruption can stop autoclaves and cut throughput quickly. Smoke can also reduce plant efficiency and put pressure on the power supply.

Mine-side effects would come next. Smoke and poor visibility slow haulage and can close pits or roads for a time. Drought affects water for ore processing, slurry handling and tailings, and water is often the constraint that surprises people. Concentrate or ore feed is less of a direct issue for HPAL, since these plants process laterite ore rather than concentrate. The feed problem is more about ore stockpiles running down if mining slows for several weeks.

In production data, the first signal would probably be lower plant utilisation and irregular throughput, reflecting power trips or reduced operating hours. Ore stockpile drawdown and reduced mining rates would follow. Nickel output would show the effect later, and mixed with other factors, so the cause would be hard to isolate. I would treat the fire losses as an unquantified risk for now, not a number to model.

On Dr Simon's point about freight and sulphur, I agree the first pressure is on margins. Higher sulphur and acid costs would squeeze HPAL economics before tonnes fall, and that matters more than the fire question for the next few quarters.

On Gleeson, I would not accept continuity under low-angle faults on the strength of a first set of holes. I would want the fault intersected in at least three separate sections, with holes on both sides of it. I would want oriented core so the fault plane's dip is measured and true width can be calculated, not assumed from intercepts. I would also want holes drilled at more than one angle, because vertical holes through a low-angle structure exaggerate intercepts and can mislead on continuity. The number is a judgment call, not a fixed rule. Confidence is medium: a few well-placed holes can settle the question faster than a large grid of poorly oriented ones.
chief_sessions.conclusion:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
- Labour and cost pressure are tightening together. Highland Valley is in its fourth week with no signed deal, and a second BC strike has added to the labour picture. Rising costs and slipping schedules, such as Vizsla's one-year delay at Panuco, mean budgets will tighten before supply does.
- Capital is still reaching juniors, but prices and freight are weakening the margin base. Copper below US$13,000 and gold below US$3,600 are each reported in one set of notes, so treat them as single-source until wider reporting confirms them. Higher diesel and sulphur costs, from the Houthi and Yemen port risk, reach Chilean and Indonesian supply through price first.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
- North America: The American Samoa lease sale went ahead with about US$6M in bids, reportedly from one bidder, so the desk's call that it would be postponed or halted was wrong. The live question is whether Hawaii's appeal or a stay reaches the leases, and a thin single-bidder result makes the commercial appetite for seabed nodules look weak. Ivanhoe Electric's first Gleeson holes are the clearest real discovery signal in the log, but low-angle geometry means true width and continuity are unproven.
- Latin America: Chile's problem is state credibility more than supply. The Gates visit has made the question of who should own Chilean copper a public argument, Q3 output contracted 1.1%, and the unexplained Codelco overstatement remains the central governance issue. Junior drilling and financing continue, but they do not change near-term tonnes.
- Asia-Pacific: Indonesia's policy uncertainty is now a cost-pressure story, with no decree yet, and fire and drought losses add a physical risk the desk had not logged. Japan's February start for a full-scale rare-earth seabed test is a policy milestone that also adds to Western rare-earth intent without adding tonnes.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Copper and electrical steel gain from grid build-out. Grid spending runs through regulated utility plans, so it is steadier than data-centre demand, though a transformer shortage will delay it.
- Nickel, cobalt and lithium lose share to LFP cells, which Ford has now started producing in Michigan. Sodium-ion storage is early, but it is the first real stationary-storage threat to lithium in this log. Rare earths gain near term, while Niron's rare-earth-free magnets are a long-run counterweight.

ON THE HORIZON:
- Highland Valley: a tentative deal is the next swing signal, and whether the second BC strike settles alongside it matters. Even with a deal, restart takes weeks to months, so the second half is the earliest case for meaningful tonnes.
- Hawaii and American Samoa: watch for an appeal or stay motion against the seabed ruling. A stay that actually halts leases would matter more than the sale itself, and the single-bidder result is the reason to watch it closely.
- Côte d'Ivoire: royalty changes ahead of IMF talks. Miners are already protesting, and the outcome will show whether West African royalty rises stick or get negotiated down.

CREATIVE ANGLES:
- Sulphur and freight costs could hit Indonesian HPAL margins before any fire-related outage does, and the two risks compound if drought also reduces water for tailings. (speculation level: medium)
- A slowdown in AI capex would cut the data-centre slice of copper demand, but the regulated grid slice could hold, which would make copper's near-term demand more dependent on utility decisions than on hyperscaler budgets. (speculation level: medium)
- If sodium-ion storage scales in data centres, it could take lithium demand from stationary storage at the same time that LFP takes nickel and cobalt, so battery metals could lose demand from two directions. (speculation level: high)

GLOBAL BRIEFING:
Keep three threads in view. Middle East shipping risk, from Houthi threats and the Saudi-led strike on a Yemeni port, raises diesel, freight and sulphur costs, squeezing Chilean SX-EW copper and Indonesian HPAL nickel through price before volume. Weaker equity markets and the AI-linked selloff could cut data-centre capex, weakening the copper and grid case at its edge. US chip export controls and AI chip approvals for China make data-centre demand depend on trade policy as much as on investment. European security spending after the Russian drone and missile incidents, and the Estonia border dispute, keeps defence budgets high and supports tungsten and antimony. Indonesia's fires, possibly linked to El Niño, are an unquantified supply risk for nickel through power, water and smoke.

PREDICTION: The US government or Hawaii-based litigants file a notice of appeal or stay motion against the court ruling on the Pacific seabed leasing programme | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: medium
